# Laws of motion (`laws_of_motion`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by falling_bodies, symbolic_algebra, calculus
- Core idea: First: a body left alone keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed; it does not need a push to keep going, and things on Earth stop only because of friction and air. Second: a force changes the motion, and the change of velocity per second equals the force divided by the mass (F = m a). Third: forces come in pairs; whatever pushes is pushed back equally (a gun recoils, a rower pushes water backwards). Uniform motion in a straight line cannot be felt, which is why we do not notice the moving Earth: a stone dropped from the mast of a smoothly sailing ship lands at the foot of the mast.
- Pitfalls:
  - Accepting the common-sense Aristotelian view that motion needs a continuing force
  - Confusing mass with weight, or force with energy or momentum
  - Stating inertia as circular motion (Galileo's own version)
  - Inventing a 'centrifugal force' that throws things outward; they simply go straight on
- History: china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – a Mohist Canon passage says motion stops only through an opposing force (reading disputed); egypt: c. 530 AD – Philoponus (Byzantine Alexandria) proposes an impressed force against Aristotle; islamic: 11th c. Ibn Sina: impressed 'mayl' would persist in a void; 12th c. Ibn Bajja and al-Baghdadi; europe: c. 1350 Buridan's impetus; 1632–1638 Galileo; 1644 Descartes states straight-line inertia; 1687 Newton's three laws
- Read:
  - Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687)
  - I. Bernard Cohen, The Birth of a New Physics (1960)
